<p class="MsoNormal">Nigeria's blue economy conversation is moving beyond the
recognition of maritime potential towards the harder question of what
institutions, infrastructure, financing and security are required to convert
that potential into sustainable economic value.</p>

<p class="MsoNormal"><o:p>&nbsp;</o:p>Nigeria has spent years identifying the scale of its
maritime opportunity.</p>

<p class="MsoNormal"><o:p>&nbsp;</o:p>The country has an extensive coastline, major ports, inland
waterways, coastal communities, marine resources and a large population whose
livelihoods are connected directly or indirectly to the water.</p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Yet possessing maritime assets is not the same as building a
maritime economy.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">That distinction increasingly defines the Ehingbeti Maritime
Hub conversation.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Established by the Ocean Ambassadors Foundation to reconnect
Lagos with its maritime heritage and examine the economic possibilities of its
waterways and coastal environment, Ehingbeti has evolved into a platform for a
much broader discussion about Nigeria's blue economy.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The earlier editions established the historical and economic
significance of Lagos' maritime identity, expanded the conversation around the
country's blue economy and increasingly brought inland waterways, investment
and coastal communities into focus.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The latest edition has taken that conversation further.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">It is now asking a more consequential question:<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">&nbsp;what architecture is
required for Nigeria's blue economy to become investable, resilient and
inclusive?<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">From Maritime Heritage to Economic Strategy<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Ehingbeti's historical foundation remains important.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal"><o:p>&nbsp;</o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The initiative takes its name from Lagos' maritime past and
seeks to reconnect contemporary economic thinking with the communities,
waterways and trading activities that shaped the development of Lagos.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal"><o:p>&nbsp;</o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">But its relevance today lies beyond history.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The evolution of Ehingbeti reflects the wider transformation
of Nigeria's maritime conversation.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The country's blue economy is no longer being discussed
simply as an untapped collection of marine resources. Increasingly, the
conversation is about the systems required to extract economic value from those
resources responsibly.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">That means infrastructure.<br>It means security.<br>It means regulation.<br>It means capital.<br>It means environmental protection.<br>And critically, it means determining how the communities
closest to the water participate in the value being created.</p>

<p class="MsoNormal"><o:p>&nbsp;</o:p>The 4th Ehingbeti Maritime Hub Summit brought these
questions together.<br>The Coastal Resilience Question.<br>One of the most significant proposals emerging from the
summit was the call for a dedicated Coastal Resilience Fund.</p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Delivering the keynote address, President of the Maritime
Arbitrators Association of Nigeria, Chief Jean Chiazor Anishere, SAN, argued
that a dedicated financing mechanism was necessary to address infrastructure
deficits and improve living conditions in coastal communities.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">She called for Nigeria to explore climate funds, development
banks and multilateral financing institutions as potential sources of capital
for coastal resilience and community development.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The proposal introduces an important dimension into the blue
economy debate. Coastal resilience is often treated as an environmental or
social concern.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">For an economy seeking to expand maritime activity, it is
also an economic infrastructure question.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal"><o:p>&nbsp;</o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal"><!--[if gte vml 1]><v:shape id="_x0000_i1026" type="#_x0000_t75"
 style='width:353.5pt;height:9in'>
 <v:imagedata src="file:///C:/Users/Isaac/AppData/Local/Temp/msohtmlclip1/01/clip_image003.jpg"
  o:title="WhatsApp Image 2026-09-19-4 at 10.02.11 AM"/>
</v:shape><![endif]--><!--[if !vml]--><img width="471" height="864" src="data:image/jpeg;base64," v:shapes="_x0000_i1026"><!--[endif]--><o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Communities exposed to environmental degradation, weak
infrastructure and inadequate public services cannot easily become stable
platforms for sustained economic activity.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The resilience of the coastal environment and the resilience
of the communities within it therefore have implications for investment.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The proposed fund remains a policy proposal. Its
significance will ultimately depend on whether it can be translated into a
credible financing structure with defined governance, funding sources,
priorities and measurable projects.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">That is where the conversation must now move.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Governance Before Capital.<br>
Anishere's intervention went beyond financing.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">She identified security, sustainability and governance as
critical pillars of Nigeria's blue economy and called for a regulatory
environment that gives investors greater certainty while protecting marine
resources and coastal populations.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal"><o:p>&nbsp;</o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">This is fundamental to the investment question.<br>
Capital responds not only to opportunity but to predictability.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Investors need to understand who regulates an activity, what
rules apply, how those rules will be enforced and what protections exist when
commercial relationships break down.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Nigeria's blue economy cuts across shipping, ports, inland
waterways, fisheries, tourism, marine services, environmental management and
security.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The challenge is therefore not simply to create more
policies.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">It is to build an institutional environment in which
existing and emerging sectors can operate with clearer mandates, fewer
regulatory uncertainties and greater coordination.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Without that architecture, the size of the opportunity
becomes less important than the difficulty of accessing it.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Security as Economic Infrastructure.<br>
The security dimension reinforces the same point.<br>
Representing the Flag Officer Commanding, Western Naval Command, Rear Admiral
N.C. Okon called for stronger maritime regulation and effective enforcement of
existing laws.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal"><o:p>&nbsp;</o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">He identified what he described as "sea blindness"
as one factor limiting Nigeria's appreciation of its maritime potential and
stressed the importance of collaboration among government agencies, coastal
communities and development partners.<br>
His intervention also linked insecurity with environmental degradation, illicit
activities and regulatory uncertainty.<br>
This matters because maritime security is not simply a defense issue. It is an
economic variable.<br>
A waterway becomes commercially useful when vessels, passengers, cargo,
infrastructure and operators can use it with reasonable confidence.<br>
Investment follows that confidence.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Without it, infrastructure can remain underutilised,
operating costs can rise and private capital can become more difficult to
attract.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Nigeria's maritime security architecture is therefore part
of its blue economy infrastructure.<br>
The Communities at the Centre<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Perhaps the most important feature of the Ehingbeti
conversation is its emphasis on coastal communities.<br>
Representing the Lagos State Governor, Permanent Secretary, Lagos State
Ministry of Tourism, Arts and Culture, Mrs. Bopo Oyekan Ismaila, said the
state's blue economy agenda extends beyond Lagos Island to communities across
Lagos.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The Chairman of the NIWA Governing Board, Alhaji Mukhtar
Shehu Shagari, represented by Capt. Tajudeen Alao, similarly stressed that
coastal communities must remain central to the implementation of blue economy
policies.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">That principle deserves closer attention.<br>
Coastal communities are not simply recipients of blue economy programmes.<br>
They already participate in maritime economic activity through fishing, water
transportation, boatbuilding, tourism, marine services and other activities.<br>
The policy challenge is how to move these activities from the margins of the
formal economy into stronger value chains.<br>
That could require access to finance, technical training, safety standards,
modern equipment, market access and opportunities to participate in larger
commercial operations.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">A genuinely inclusive blue economy should therefore ask not
only how much investment enters coastal areas, but also how much local
capability, ownership and income is created as a result.<br>
The Inland Waterways Opportunity.<br>
The inland waterways discussion carries forward one of the strongest themes in
Ehingbeti's evolution.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Convener Hon. Olaitan Violet Williams described Nigeria's
inland waterways as one of the country's significant blue economy opportunities
and called for greater investment and stronger legal protection for investors. She
cited an estimated 10,000 kilometers of waterways while noting that their
economic potential remains constrained by poor navigability.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The real issue, however, is not the length of Nigeria's
waterways. It is their functionality.<br>
<br>
A waterway becomes an economic asset when it can support predictable movement,
connect communities to markets, carry passengers and cargo, support tourism and
create commercially viable marine services. This is where inland waterways
intersect with Nigeria's wider logistics and trade ambitions.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">A better functioning inland waterway system could diversify
transport options, connect underserved communities and create new markets
around transportation, marine services, tourism, fisheries and related
activities.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The opportunity is therefore much larger than passenger
transportation alone.<br>
From Opportunity to Investment<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The launch of the 28 Inland Waterways Investment Jigsaw at
the summit represents an attempt to give greater structure to that opportunity.<br>
<br>
The initiative is designed to identify viable investment opportunities across
Nigeria's inland waterways and provide a pathway for greater private sector
participation. <o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The next question is whether those opportunities can become
investable projects.<br>
An investor needs more than an identified location or a description of an
opportunity.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">There must be clarity around ownership, regulation,
infrastructure requirements, security, environmental obligations, revenue
models, community participation and financing structures.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">This is the difference between identifying potential and
developing an investment pipeline.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The Jigsaw therefore has the opportunity to become an
important bridge between policy ambition and private capital if the identified
opportunities are developed into projects that can withstand commercial and
financial scrutiny.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The Risk Architecture:<br>
The intervention by Ekeoma Ezeibe, Chairman of the Nigerian Council of
Registered Insurance Brokers, added another layer to the conversation.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">She identified insurance as a critical component of maritime
and blue economy development, particularly in protecting maritime assets,
infrastructure and businesses against operational and marine risks.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">That is an important part of the investment equation.<br>
Capital does not enter maritime infrastructure without considering risk.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Insurance provides one mechanism for transferring and
managing some of those risks, while strengthening the overall financial
architecture around marine investment.<br>
The emergence of a stronger blue economy therefore requires more than investors
and projects.<br>
It requires a functioning ecosystem of finance, insurance, regulation,
infrastructure and security.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal"><o:p>&nbsp;</o:p></p>

<h2><span class="Heading2Char"><span style="font-size:14.0pt;
line-height:115%">What Ehingbeti Is Becoming? <br>
</span></span><br>
The evolution of Ehingbeti is itself instructive.<br>
Its origins lie in maritime history and the desire to reconnect Lagos with the
waterways that helped shape its identity.<o:p></o:p></h2>

<p class="MsoNormal">The conversation then expanded into the wider blue economy,
bringing greater attention to marine resources, inland waterways and economic
opportunities.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">It has now reached a more difficult stage. The question is
no longer simply what Nigeria's blue economy could become.<br>
It is what must be built around it for that potential to become durable
economic activity.<br>
That requires a shift from awareness to architecture.<br>
From conferences to projects.<br>
From potential to bankability.<br>
From communities as beneficiaries to communities as participants.<br>
From isolated interventions to coordinated institutions.<br>
And from maritime assets as geographical features to maritime assets as
productive economic infrastructure.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal"><span class="Heading2Char"><span style="font-size:14.0pt;
line-height:115%">From Proposals to Implementation.</span></span><br>
The Coastal Resilience Fund, the Inland Waterways Investment Jigsaw and the
wider calls for regulatory and security reforms all point in the same
direction.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Nigeria now needs mechanisms that can convert these ideas
into implementation.<br>
The Coastal Resilience Fund requires a defined institutional and financing
structure.<br>
The Inland Waterways Investment Jigsaw needs to produce projects that investors
and financial institutions can assess.<br>
The regulatory conversation needs to identify specific barriers and the
institutions responsible for addressing them.<br>
<br>
The security agenda requires sustained coordination between government
agencies, communities and maritime operators.<br>
And the inclusion of coastal communities needs to be reflected in how projects
are designed, financed and measured.<br>
This is the point at which the blue economy conversation becomes more
demanding.<br>
Announcements can establish direction.<br>
Implementation establishes economic value.<o:p></o:p></p>

<h2>PrimeAxis Insight<o:p></o:p></h2>

<p class="MsoNormal">Ehingbeti's significance lies increasingly in the questions
it is forcing Nigeria to confront.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The country does not lack maritime potential.<br>
It lacks sufficient conversion mechanisms between that potential and economic
value.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">A coastline does not automatically create a blue economy.<br>
Waterways do not become logistics corridors simply because they exist.<br>
Communities do not become economically empowered merely because they are
located beside valuable maritime assets.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">And investment does not flow simply because an opportunity
has been identified.<br>
The architecture matters.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Nigeria needs secure maritime spaces, navigable waterways,
resilient coastal infrastructure, predictable regulation, credible financing
structures, effective risk protection and stronger pathways for local
participation.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal"><o:p>&nbsp;</o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The 4th Ehingbeti conversation brings these elements into
one frame.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">That may ultimately prove more important than any individual
announcement from the summit.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">The next measure of progress should therefore be practical.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Can the Coastal Resilience Fund move from proposal to
structure?<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Can the Inland Waterways Investment Jigsaw move from
opportunity mapping to bankable projects?<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Can regulatory and security reforms reduce the uncertainty
facing investors?<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Can coastal communities gain meaningful access to the
economic value being created around them?<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">These are the questions that will determine whether
Nigeria's blue economy remains a compelling national ambition or develops into
a functioning economic ecosystem.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal">Ehingbeti has helped keep the maritime conversation
connected to the communities, waterways and history from which it emerged.<br>
<br>
Its next challenge is to help connect that conversation to capital,
infrastructure, institutions and implementation.<br>
<br>
That is where Nigeria's blue economy becomes more than potential.<br>
That is where it becomes an economy.<o:p></o:p></p>

<p class="MsoNormal"><o:p>&nbsp;</o:p></p>
